summaries.example: Imagine asking for rain for a garden. It rains the next day, but we do not yet know whether the rain came partly because someone prayed or whether it would have rained anyway. Philosophers call the prayer effective only in the first kind of case.
summaries.summary: Petitionary prayer means asking God or another special being for something. The entry studies puzzles about prayer in traditional monotheism, where God is described as perfectly good, all-knowing, unchanging, and able to do anything that is possible. One major question is what it means for a prayer to be answered. Many philosophers say the prayer must help bring about the requested event, not merely happen before it. This raises problems: how could prayer influence an unchanging God? How could it affect a future already known by God? Would a perfectly good God need anyone to ask before doing what is best? Philosophers offer different answers. Some change their account of God's knowledge or changeability. Others say prayer can support human responsibility, caring relationships, or community. The entry also asks whether people can know that a particular prayer was answered and discusses the limits of studies that try to test prayer statistically.
key_ideas: An answered prayer might mean more than a requested event happening; many philosophers ask whether the prayer helped cause it.
If God cannot change or be affected, it is difficult to explain how a prayer could influence God.
If God already knows the future, philosophers ask how a later prayer could make a difference.
Some thinkers say prayer can have value by building responsibility, community, or a relationship with God.
People may find it difficult to know whether a particular event happened because of a prayer.
summaries.why_it_matters: Prayer is important in many religions, and thinking carefully about it helps us understand ideas about God, freedom, goodness, cause and effect, and knowledge. The topic also teaches us not to jump from “this happened after I asked” to “my asking caused it.”

important_terms.definition: A prayer in which someone asks a special being, such as God, for something.
A prayer is effective when the requested event happens partly because the prayer influenced God to act.
The idea that God knows everything that can be known, including questions about the future.
The belief that God cannot change.
The belief that nothing outside God can affect God.
The study of how we know things or when a belief is reasonable.

questions_to_think_about: If you ask for something and it happens, what would show that your request made a difference?
Could a prayer matter even if it did not change what God was going to do?
If someone knows what you will choose tomorrow, are you still choosing freely?
Can people always tell why an event happened?

summaries.example: Suppose a student prays that a friend will recover, and the friend does recover. On a difference-making account, this is not enough for an answered prayer: the recovery must have occurred partly because of the prayer, rather than through independent medical or providential reasons. Yet the student may reasonably interpret the event differently depending on broader beliefs about divine action and whether such connections can be known.
summaries.summary: The entry examines whether petitionary prayer can be effective within traditional monotheism. An influential account says that God answers a petition only if the requested event occurs partly because the petition was offered; mere temporal sequence is insufficient. This definition creates several tensions. If God is immutable and impassible, prayer seems unable to alter divine action. If God is omniscient, especially if God knows a detailed future, it is unclear how a later human request could make a difference. Proposed solutions include open theism, which limits knowledge of unsettled future choices; middle knowledge, which combines knowledge of what creatures would freely do with knowledge of the actual world; timeless eternity, in which God knows history non-temporally; and theological determinism, in which God determines events. A further issue concerns moral perfection: perhaps God would do what is best without requests, but some philosophers argue that waiting for prayer can foster responsibility, community, dependence, or a genuine divine-human partnership. Finally, the entry asks whether anyone can justifiably know that a particular prayer was answered. General religious belief may support such judgments for some thinkers, while skeptical approaches emphasize our limited access to God's reasons. Empirical research is also difficult because prayer cannot easily be isolated as the only relevant cause.
key_ideas: The standard causal analysis of answered prayer requires more than coincidence: the petition must be part of the explanation for God's action.
Divine immutability and impassibility appear to leave no room for prayer to alter God's action, though theists may revise or reinterpret those doctrines.
Omniscience creates a problem about whether a prayer can affect a future God already knows; open theism, middle knowledge, timeless eternity, and theological determinism offer different responses.
Divine moral perfection raises the question of why God would wait for requests, but proposed answers appeal to human responsibility, dependence, community, freedom, or the value of relationship.
Epistemic uncertainty remains: even when a request is followed by its fulfillment, independent divine reasons may explain the event.
Statistical studies face difficulties, including controlling whether people prayed and treating God as if divine action followed a fixed natural law.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate connects religious practice with major philosophical questions about causation, freedom, foreknowledge, moral perfection, evidence, and interpretation. It also models how to analyze a claim carefully: define “answered,” separate correlation from explanation, and recognize that different accounts of God produce different arguments.

important_terms.definition: A request directed toward God or another being regarded as having special status.
Prayer understood causally: God brings about the requested result partly because the prayer was offered.
The view that God knows everything that can be known; a central dispute concerns whether this includes a fully settled future.
The doctrine that God does not change. It differs from impassibility, although immutability would imply it in the framework discussed.
The doctrine that God cannot be affected by anything external.
The philosophical study of knowledge, justification, and reasonable belief.
A view that God does not know future actions that are not yet settled, including some free human choices.
A view according to which God knows what creatures would freely do in possible situations and knows which situation becomes actual.

questions_to_think_about: Is an event an answered prayer if the prayer did not make a causal difference but had personal or relational significance?
Does foreknowledge make a future event fixed, or can God know a free choice without determining it?
Would a perfectly good God have reasons to make some benefits depend on petitionary prayer?
What evidence could distinguish divine response from coincidence or an independent cause?
Are experiments on intercessory prayer capable of testing a free divine agent?

summaries.example: A teenager asks God to help a team win, and the team wins. One philosopher might say the prayer was answered only if God gave the team some help because of the request. Another might say the prayer can count as answered if the person’s main goal was to feel connected with God, even if the request did not change God's reasons.
summaries.summary: Petitionary prayer is prayer that asks for something. The entry focuses on philosophical questions about whether such prayer can really affect God and events in the world. Many philosophers use a demanding definition of an answered prayer: the requested result must happen partly because the prayer was made. Other philosophers think this definition may be too strict, since people may care about connection with God rather than about changing divine action. Traditional monotheism describes God as all-knowing, perfectly good, unchanging, and unable to be affected from outside. These qualities create puzzles. If God cannot change, how can a request influence God? If God knows the future, how can a later prayer alter what will happen? The entry presents several responses, including open theism, middle knowledge, timeless eternity, and theological determinism. It also considers whether God's goodness would make prayer unnecessary. Some philosophers argue that God could have reasons to make certain goods depend on requests, such as encouraging responsibility, community, freedom, or partnership. Others question whether this is compatible with perfect goodness. The final issue is knowledge: even when a requested event occurs, people may not be able to tell whether prayer caused it. Studies of prayer face challenges because researchers cannot easily prevent outside prayers or treat divine action as an automatic force.
key_ideas: Philosophers disagree about what “answered prayer” should mean: causal influence may be required, or the meaning may depend on what the person is asking about.
A God who is unchanging or unaffected seems unable to respond to a new request, but some thinkers revise these ideas or describe prayer as part of a larger plan.
Different theories of God's knowledge of the future lead to different answers about whether prayer can influence events.
Some arguments say prayer helps people grow in responsibility, avoid thinking they are completely self-sufficient, and care for one another.
Knowing that something happened after a prayer does not by itself prove that the prayer caused it.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters to religious people who pray and to anyone interested in how explanations work. It shows why a simple experience can raise difficult questions about cause, chance, freedom, goodness, and evidence. It also encourages respectful thinking about disagreements within philosophy of religion.

important_terms.definition: A prayer that asks God or another sacred being for a particular thing.
Prayer that makes a difference by helping bring about what was requested.
Knowing everything that can be known. Philosophers debate whether an unknowable, unsettled future can already be known.
Not changing. In the discussion, divine immutability means that God does not change.
Not being changed by anything outside oneself. This is related to, but not exactly the same as, immutability.
A reason or cause for doing something; philosophers ask whether a prayer can give God a reason to act.
A view that some future choices, especially free human choices, are not settled facts for God to know in advance.
A theory that God knows what people would freely do in every possible situation and uses this knowledge in planning the actual world.

questions_to_think_about: Should an answered prayer require that God changed course because of the request?
Can a person be free if God already knows what that person will do?
Why might someone think it is better for God to wait for a request?
What problems arise when researchers compare people who receive prayer with people who supposedly do not?
Could praying for a past event make sense under some theories of divine knowledge?
